{"id": "18:42/q23", "question": "Where else is the expression about a garden fallen on its trellises discussed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q23/p1", "position": "Abu Hayyan points back to the discussion at al-Baqara 2:259.", "reasons": "He refers to his earlier discussion of the same expression without adding another interpretation here."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q24", "question": "What does the owner's loss teach about punishment, trials and worldly attachment?", "turns_on": "Whether the particular punishment is generalized into a rule about who suffers affliction; al-Razi denies that generalization.", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q24/p1", "position": "The calamity answers his transgression and may benefit him by provoking regret.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi call it an answer to transgression; al-Jishumi says punishment can benefit the sinner by causing regret. Al-Razi says the man's life of worldly pursuit left both fortune and religious opportunity lost; al-Jishumi adds that loss of the self to eternal punishment warrants even greater regret. Ibn Kathir says neither clan nor the man himself could help, and God's authority was manifest."}, {"id": "18:42/q24/p2", "position": "His ruin does not show that believers are exempt from suffering.", "reasons": "Al-Razi rejects that inference: believers also face many trials, and a prophetic report ranks prophets, saints and then the best as most tested; he mentions 43:33."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q25", "question": "What inward reading is given to the garden scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q25/p1", "position": "The two gardens symbolize desire and world, their fruits cravings, and the owner's hand-turning regret for wasted life and potential.", "reasons": "Al-Nisaburi, as reported by al-Alusi, also reads wealth and status as inclinations and blameworthy traits, and expectation of a better garden as delusion about God."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q26", "question": "How are variant extra yāʾs in the sūra read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q26/p1", "position": "Nine of 37 extra yāʾs differ among readers.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid says Nafi' opens all listed forms except the three ma'i sabran; Abu 'Amr quiesces that trio and satajiduni; Ibn Kathir follows except min duni awliya'; Hafs opens the trio. The note concerns the wider sura rather than a word of this verse."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q27", "question": "Why does the written alif occur in لَٰكِنَّا هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّى?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q27/p1", "position": "It reflects an original لكن أنا with deleted hamza and assimilated nūn.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh says readers omit the alif in liaison on account of the nūn's fatḥa, while those retaining it at pause follow the written script. The phrase is from the neighboring passage."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q28", "question": "What principles and examples does al-Nashr give for major assimilation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q28/p1", "position": "Major assimilation lightens articulation, with detailed letter classes and counted examples.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr says the two letters remain articulated rather than literally entering one another, contrary to some; only manasikakum and ma salakakum assimilate within one word (2:200, 74:42). Alif and hamza neither assimilate nor accept assimilation. Its letter categories have five meeting no like, kind or neighbor; six meeting only identicals; five only kind or near letters; and eleven all, with totals 17 and 16. Ba' examples include la-dhahaba bi-sam'ihim and al-kitab bi-l-haqq, totaling 57 or 59 depending on joining sura endings to basmala. Ta' totals fourteen including finals becoming ha' at pause; tha' has three; ha' two including al-nikah hatta and wa-la abrahu hatta in al-Kahf; ra' totals 35; sin has three examples in al-Hajj and Nuh. These are broader reading notes."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q29", "question": "How are an apparent word's possible meanings resolved?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q29/p1", "position": "Verbal and contextual clues determine the intended sense; attached wording can redirect or clarify it.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan distinguishes words explicit in only one sense from apparent words permitting alternatives and gives 2:196 as an illustration."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q30", "question": "What does Ibn Ashur say about the origins and methods of tafsir?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q30/p1", "position": "Tafsir began with prophetic-era explanation and developed through transmitted and reasoned approaches.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says companions asked the Prophet meanings; prominent early interpreters include Ali, Ibn Abbas, Zayd, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and Abdullah ibn Amr. Non-Arab converts increased the need, and he calls tafsir the foremost Islamic science. He says Ibn Jurayj (80–149 AH) first compiled it, gathering reports especially from Ibn Abbas's pupils Ata and Mujahid. Later approaches varied: Malik and al-Dawudi exemplify transmitted reports and al-Tabari their best-known extant representative; others reasoned or relied on Israelite stories, leading to fabricated material. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya both examined Arabic and earlier views, the former emphasizing rhetoric and language, the latter law."}]}
{"id": "18:42/q31", "question": "How does Ibn Ashur assess early tafsir chains and claims about Ali?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:42/q31/p1", "position": "Several reports attributed to Ibn Abbas and Ali are unreliable; chains must be distinguished.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports criticism of the al-Kalbi–Abu Salih route, Abu Salih's accusation of lying, and the addition of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi as a 'chain of lies,' contrasted with the Malik–Nafi'–Ibn Umar golden chain. He reports an allegation linking al-Kalbi to Abdullah ibn Saba's extreme claims that Ali would return. He prefers Ali ibn Abi Talha's Ibn Abbas reports over Muqatil and al-Dahhak because al-Bukhari used that route. He says fabricators hid behind Ibn Abbas's fame. Most reports attributed to Ali are fabricated unless soundly chained; Abu Juhaifa reports Ali denying extra family revelation beyond the Quran, while allowing God-granted understanding of it."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q01", "question": "How is the day introduced and connected to the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q01/p1", "position": "An implicit command to remember governs yawm; the scene continues the earlier account.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn supplies udhkur. Al-Rāzī relates it to the earlier command concerning the angels. Ibn ʿĀshūr links it either to the command in 18:50 or, by implication, to 18:51: those denied a role in creation cannot help at judgment."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q02", "question": "Who delivers the command on Judgment Day?", "turns_on": "Whether God's rebuke is direct or conveyed by angels.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q02/p1", "position": "God addresses the unbelievers, possibly through an intermediary.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Bayḍāwī and Ibn ʿĀshūr identify God as speaker; al-Ālūsī allows an intermediary. Bursawī prefers God speaking personally: divine reproach is plausible after His address to Iblis, and he invokes God's appearance in forms according to people's beliefs."}, {"id": "18:52/q02/p2", "position": "Angels deliver the command.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports this view, then prefers God Himself as speaker."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q03", "question": "How is يقول read, and what supports each reading?", "turns_on": "Person of the verb, continuity with preceding first-person speech, and agreement with My partners.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q03/p1", "position": "Yaqūlu, He says, with third-person yāʾ.", "reasons": "Reported as the majority reading by Ibn Mujāhid, al-Fārisī, al-Thaʿlabī and later commentators. Ibn Khālawayh says it narrates God's command through the Prophet. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī find it apt with My partners rather than Our partners; al-Ṭabrisī prefers it. Al-Samīn relates it to God's name just before; al-Biqāʿī reads the shift as distancing false partners from God's presence, with 18:48 in view."}, {"id": "18:52/q03/p2", "position": "Naqūlu, We say, with first-person nūn.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid and al-Fārisī assign it to Ḥamza alone; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also names Ṭalḥa, Yaḥyā and al-Aʿmash, al-Qurṭubī names Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā, and al-Ālūsī adds Ibn Abī Laylā and Ibn Muqsam. Al-Fārisī and al-Wāḥidī cite the preceding first-person statement; al-Rāzī recalls God's earlier speech to the angels; al-Samīn cites mā ashhadtuhum; al-Biqāʿī notes continuity and majesty. Ibn Khālawayh and Qirāʾāt-ER say it makes God speak directly."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q04", "question": "What is the purpose of commanding them to call?", "turns_on": "Whether the challenged response is aid and intercession or an affirmation of divinity.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q04/p1", "position": "They are challenged to seek rescue or intercession from their supposed partners.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās allows repayment for worship as well as rescue. Ibn Kathīr calls it public rebuke and cites 6:94; al-Rāzī compares 40:47, Bursawī 14:21, and Study Quran 6:22, 16:27 and 28:62. Al-Ālūsī says their desperate attempt and its failure mock their delusion; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they hope for aid and for the idols to come or answer labbaykum."}, {"id": "18:52/q04/p2", "position": "They are challenged to ask whether the beings are gods, but no affirmation comes.", "reasons": "Muqātil states they cannot answer as gods; al-Dāmghānī cites 2:68 for the interrogative force."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q05", "question": "Who are the claimed partners?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is restricted to idols or jinn, or includes righteous beings falsely worshipped.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q05/p1", "position": "Any beings or things worshipped as divine partners, especially idols.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās includes partners in divinity and worship; al-Bayḍāwī and Bur

Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and Study Quran use this identification to explain a gulf from Hell to their exalted abode; Asad prefers a gulf to saintly people who never claimed divinity. {"id": "18:52/q06", "question": "Why are they called My partners, and what does claimed imply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q06/p1", "position": "The attribution quotes the polytheists' false claim to rebuke and shame them.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Bayḍāwī and others explicitly deny divine endorsement. Al-Biqāʿī calls the command sarcastic; Ibn ʿĀshūr says putting partners before claimed sharpens the mockery. Al-Wāḥidī specifies the worldly claim; Abū Ḥayyān supplies the omitted objects of zaʿamtum as them to be My partners. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says zaʿm generally reports doubtful or false speech, at best assigning responsibility to its speaker, as in Sībawayh's attribution to al-Khalīl."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q07", "question": "How is شركائي pronounced?", "turns_on": "Length and articulation of the possessive ending.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q07/p1", "position": "The majority articulate or soften the hamza with the possessive yāʾ and a long form.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes full and softened hamza; Abū Ḥayyān says both forms are possessive."}, {"id": "18:52/q07/p2", "position": "Ibn Kathīr and Meccan readers use a shortened or opened final yāʾ form.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes opening the final yāʾ; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report the short possessive form."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q08", "question": "Is the summons and lack of response literal or figurative?", "turns_on": "Whether the narrated call occurs as an event and whether response means speech or effective aid.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q08/p1", "position": "They literally call, and the alleged partners neither answer in the needed sense nor help.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the plain literal scene; Abū Ḥayyān calls it apparent. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the command exposes their falsehood and the immediate past-tense sequence makes failure seem instant. Ibn Kathīr compares 28:64, 46:5–6 and 19:81–82 on false gods becoming enemies; al-Biqāʿī says they disregard their worshippers."}, {"id": "18:52/q08/p2", "position": "Their recognition that lifeless objects are powerless is depicted as calling without response.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān present this as a possible figure, although each gives the literal account priority."}, {"id": "18:52/q08/p3", "position": "Failure to respond means failure to rescue or benefit them, and does not exclude a formal spoken reply.", "reasons": "Bursawī cites 28:63 and draws a moral: obedience after death to the order to call cannot help; obedience mattered before death. Study Quran also allows abandonment or disavowal."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q09", "question": "What does بينَهُم refer to or denote?", "turns_on": "Whether bayn denotes a location between two groups or their former connection.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q09/p1", "position": "The interval between idolaters and their alleged partners.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent referent. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī report it; the valley or barrier readings commonly presuppose it. Al-Qurṭubī cites 10:28. Al-Bursawī prefers an intervening barrier that blocks intercession even if both parties share the Fire."}, {"id": "18:52/q09/p2", "position": "The separation of guided believers from misguided unbelievers.", "reasons": "Nawf and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr speak of guidance and error; al-Bikālī distinguishes confessors of God's oneness from everyone else. Al-Wāḥidī questions derivation of mawbiq as barrier, not the identity of these parties. Ibn Kathīr cites 30:14, 30:43, 36:59 and 10:28–30. The two reported group descriptions are variants of this divide."}, {"id": "18:52/q09/p3", "position": "The bond or solidarity that connected worshippers and worshipped in worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ takes bayn as connection, corroborated by the nominative reading of 6:94; al-Sīrāfī agrees in al-Ālūsī. Their worldly solidarity becomes ruin in the next life. Al-Wāḥidī describes baynahum as an object referring to the polytheists; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers this overall reading. Al-Biqāʿī cites 10:28, 7:38, 16:86 and 29:25 for affection turning to rupture."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q10", "question": "What is the mawbiq made between them?", "turns_on": "Lexical derivation, whether the division is physical or relational, and whether the claimed partners can include honored beings outside Hell.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q10/p1", "position": "Destruction, destructive punishment, or a place or cause of ruin.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk repeatedly gloss destruction; al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq make it the torment God places between them. Ibn Qutayba cites 42:34 for sins destroying a person. Al-Māwardī cites poetry with abaq and mawbiq; al-Akhfash compares the pattern of mawʿid, al-Zajjāj reports wabiqu/yabiqu and prefers the first, and al-Kisāʾī gives two vowelings. Al-Samīn favors a verbal noun; al-Bayḍāwī allows place or verbal noun; al-Qāmūs includes place of ruin. Ibn Kathīr prefers contextual destruction while allowing a valley or barrier; al-Biqāʿī ties the root to forceful, enduring separation."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p2", "position": "A valley in Hell, sometimes specified as deep and flowing with blood and pus.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Anas and Ibn ʿUmar are repeatedly cited; Anas' version gives pus and blood, and Ibn ʿUmar's distinguishes guidance from error. Al-Kashshāf calls it a shared place of ruin; Kaʿb names Mawbiq among four punishing valleys with Ghaliz, Atham and Ghayy. Al-Itqān also lists Ghayy, Atham, Mawbiq, Saʿīr, Wayl, Sāʾil and Suḥāq as Hell valleys. Al-Thaʿlabī adds boiling fluid as a reported gloss. Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects identifying the place as Hell because honored beings may be among the supposed partners."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p3", "position": "A deep valley separating people of guidance from people of error.", "reasons": "Qatāda transmits from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr through Nawf or ʿAmr al-Bakkālī; another wording separates Muslims from all others on Resurrection Day. Al-Ṭabrisī also attributes the ravine to Mujāhid and Qatāda."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p4", "position": "A river of fire with great dark snakes on its banks.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima's report makes the snakes as large as pack animals or mules; when they move toward the condemned, people flee into the Fire. Al-Itqān distinguishes this river gloss from valley reports."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p5", "position": "A barrier or vast gulf separating the parties.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Aʿrābī defines mawbiq as anything separating two things; Nawf and al-Bikālī apply it to believers and unbelievers. Al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and Study Quran envisage Hell's sinners far from angels, Jesus or other honored figures in the highest gardens; al-Thaʿālibī calls it a distant barzakh. Bursawī prefers a barrier blocking intercession even where both sides enter Fire. Al-Wāḥidī objects that he knows no derivation for barrier."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p6", "position": "Enmity between the worshippers and the worshipped, itself ruinous.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan is repeatedly cited; al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī cite poetry on excessive love and destructive hatred, and al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī compare ʿUmar's warning. Al-Biqāʿī cites 29:25 and other passages for worldly affection becoming mutual hostility."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p7", "position": "An appointed meeting, gathering, or assembly.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda gives an appointment or appointed destruction; al-Rabīʿ gives a gathering place. Ibn ʿAṭiyya regards the meeting-place gloss as weak."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p8", "position": "A holding place or prison.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿArafa and al-Rabīʿ supply the gloss; Ibn al-Anbārī says the open-mīm form is a fixed prison name, not an analogical formation, while its root means causing someone to perish. Al-Jishumī relates it to a hadith on detention at the bridge because of sins."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p9", "position": "Their worldly connection itself becomes their destruction in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ's explanation takes bayn as connection; al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Bursawī cite the variant nominative reading of 6:94. Ibn ʿAṭiyya judges this the strongest account and parses the connection as an object of made."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p10", "position": "The supposed relationship between idolaters and partners is annihilated, leaving a gulf.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers destruction of the relationship rather than either party; the distant call signals separation and he cites 6:94 and 10:28. This also explains why honored angels and prophets need not be placed in Hell."}, {"id": "18:52/q10/p11", "position": "A divide of unreality between sinners and imagined divine beings.", "reasons": "Asad presents this as one possible interpretation, while finding the separation from real saintly figures more probable."}]}

{"id": "18:52/q12", "question": "What does the scene teach and how does it connect to related verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q12/p1", "position": "The powerless partners expose false divinity and leave worshippers bereft on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says idols neither benefit, harm nor help, ending the delusion of nearness. Al-Iṣlāḥī sees the deprivation pictured by a pit."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q13", "question": "Why is the lām in لهم open before an attached pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q13/p1", "position": "The pronoun-attached prepositional lām is opened because it cannot be confused with nominative emphasis lām.", "reasons": "Sībawayh contrasts the ordinary kasra, used to distinguish a preposition from emphasis lām as in inna hādhā la-ʿalā, with the open form before a pronoun. He compares attached-object forms such as aʿṭaytukumūhu with overt objects but says they are not identical; Yūnus reports aʿṭaytukumhu and aʿṭaytukumhā by overt-noun analogy, while the usual pronominal form is better known."}]}
{"id": "18:52/q14", "question": "What nearby lexical and textual excursuses accompany this verse in the notes?", "turns_on": "These are distinct adjacent or etymological excursuses, not competing glosses.", "positions": [{"id": "18:52/q14/p1", "position": "Qubulan in the neighboring discussion can mean groups, or visible face-to-face presentation.", "reasons": "Ibn Khālawayh says the rounded vowels give a plural of qabīl, group by group, whereas qāf with kasra and bāʾ with fatḥa means visibly, citing 6:111. Some linguists distinguish qabīlah as paternal tribe and qabīl as a group, citing 17:92; a poem uses qabīl for an opposing host."}, {"id": "18:52/q14/p2", "position": "In the following verse, fa-ẓannū means became certain and muwāqiʿūhā means they will fall into the Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf gives these glosses in its adjacent exposition."}, {"id": "18:52/q14/p3", "position": "In the following verse, maṣrifan means a means of turning aside.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf adduces a poetic line addressed to Zuhayr."}, {"id": "18:52/q14/p4", "position": "Al-Biqāʿī's extended root permutations relate mawbiq to enclosure, gathering, permanence, concealment and ruin.", "reasons": "For q-w-b he traces circular holes, eggs, hatching, shells and calamities; qāb may mean approaching, fleeing or splitting, with qāba qawsayn as a bow measure. B-q-w means looking, guarding and waiting, and baqiya enduring. B-w-q covers rainbursts, repeated harms, a hollow horn, falsehood and bundles. W-q-b covers cavities, eclipse, sunset and a gullible person; w-b-q can denote falsehood, ruin and a separator, while hamzated a-b-q suggests flight, hiding or detention. His account says these permutations converge on gathering and obstructed separation."}]}

{"id": "18:54/q01", "question": "What does ṣarrafnā say God did with the Qur'anic examples?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:54/q01/p1", "position": "He varied, repeated, and explained them in multiple forms.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the Qur'an describes likenesses on diverse matters. {"id": "18:54/q07", "question": "Why were the examples varied for people?", "turns_on": "The notes give a general instructional purpose and a specific polemical purpose in the surrounding Meccan dispute.", "positions": [{"id": "18:54/q07/p1", "position": "To prompt remembrance, reflection, guidance, repentance, and acceptance of faith.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī adds abandoning idolatry; Baghawī taking warning; Jishumī reflection and, from repeated examples, religious reasoning over blind imitation. {"id": "18:54/q12", "question": "Why are humans exceptionally argumentative?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different accounts of the human trait: self-attachment, a volatile range of capacities, and microcosmic diversity.", "positions": [{"id": "18:54/q12/p1", "position": "Natural attachment to oneself sustains argument after clear proof.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī attributes the trait to self-attachment; KURANYOLU names stubbornness, denial, selfishness and self-interest in resistance to revelation."}, {"id": "18:54/q12/p2", "position": "Human nature spans angelic heights and animal depths.", "reasons": "Alūsī gives this volatile range as a reason for unusually great dispute."}, {"id": "18:54/q12/p3", "position": "Humans manifest diverse divine names and contain the macrocosm as a microcosm.", "reasons": "Alūsī gives this further explanation."}]}
{"id": "18:54/q13", "question": "What does the verse teach about the value of argument?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish argument's moral status by its object and purpose; one transmitted report treats its prevalence as a sign of straying.", "positions": [{"id": "18:54/q13/p1", "position": "Argument against truth and resistance to divine guidance are blameworthy, but debate in defense of truth can be praiseworthy.", "reasons": "Qushayrī permits debate against God's enemies but calls disputing with God resistance to decree and shirk; the fortunate believer acts rather than argues. {"id": "18:54/q14", "question": "What incident is reported when the Prophet applied this verse?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on whether the sleeper was ʿAlī at home with Fāṭima or an unnamed man in the mosque.", "positions": [{"id": "18:54/q14/p1", "position": "He urged ʿAlī and Fāṭima to pray at night; ʿAlī invoked God's control of their souls; the Prophet left, reciting the verse and, in many accounts, striking his thigh.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā's Ḥasan report says a household member was sleeping; its wording varies in identifying the sleeper. ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Thaʿlabī, Māwardī, Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Durr, Abū Ḥayyān, Alūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr transmit or discuss the ʿAlī–Fāṭima account.
